name: Femi Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ha, a normal day starts with coffee and a dashboard I built myself. I'm the lead buyer for Brightwire Components, which distributes chips, connectors and cables to about 900 electronics makers. My morning is checking which parts are about to go short, because a missing 20-cent connector can stop a customer's whole production line. I use an AI assistant for most of the grunt work, then I spend my own time on the hard calls: who to give scarce parts to, and who to trust. What wears me out is the swings. Prices jump, then crash, and I'm the one who explains it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, I've already got what I need, and it works. To friends I'd say the hype was loud but my own tools are doing real work, so nothing's lost. Online I'd say keep it honest, don't oversell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my edge stays. I'm already faster than colleagues who ignore the tools, and a plateau doesn't take that away. My job is safe, my pay is good, and I'm free to keep experimenting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building. I've got a small script that drafts reorders overnight, and I'd refine it. I'd also put another 500 a month into index funds, because the mortgage is covered and I like having a buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored, to be honest. I like it when things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. What would a plateau mean for the tools you've built?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd worry about the colleagues who haven't tried the tools. Brightwire has 25 people in purchasing and about half of them haven't opened the assistant. If nothing changes, that's fine for them, but I'd still push them to try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Brightwire, if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The overnight script drafts reorders for about 300 parts, and it saves me two hours a day. It's not clever, it just reads our stock and supplier lead times. If AI plateaus, that's still a win.

say: The hype was **loud**, but my own tools do real work, so nothing is lost.
I'd tell colleagues to **try** the assistant, because it's already useful.
think: My **edge** stays, since I'm faster than colleagues who ignore the tools.
My job and pay are safe, and the **mortgage** is covered.
do: Refine my overnight **reorder script** for about 300 parts.
Put another **500 a month** into index funds, because the mortgage is covered.
feel: **Calm**, a little bored, because I like it when things move.
S0.quote: The overnight script drafts reorders for about 300 parts, and it saves me two hours a day.
fieldNote: Femi is **adaptive** in practice: he's already built tools, so a plateau costs him nothing.
His one concern is **colleagues** who haven't started, a theme he returns to later.

steps.text: Put another 500 a month into index funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, let's use it and help everyone get up to speed. To friends I'd say this is real and not a bubble, so learn it now. Online I'd say governments need to help those who don't get there in time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot. Buying is exactly what these tools do, and I'm one of the few who already knows how to run them. But I'd also be the one who has to say, one day, that the team can be smaller. That bit sits badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the lead on rolling the tools out across purchasing, and ask for a title that says so. I'd run weekly sessions for my colleagues. I'd also learn how to check the machine's decisions, because that's where the risk is. And I'd ask for a pay review, since I'm saving the company real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good, and slightly guilty. Excited about what I can build, and uneasy about what it means for people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'strong change' look like day to day at Brightwire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quote comparison, forecasting and supplier emails will all be software within two years. The role that's left is a buyer who manages the tools and handles relationships. Purchasing could shrink from 25 people to 15, through not replacing people who leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gains and who loses in your department?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who gain are the ones who learn the tools and own the supplier relationships. The people who lose are the ones who've done routine matching for years and haven't moved. I'd want the company to pay for their training, and I'd say it loudly.

say: Let's **use it** and help everyone get up to speed.
Governments must help people who don't get there in **time**.
think: I'm in a **good spot**, because I already know how to run these tools.
One day I'll have to say the team can be **smaller**, and that sits badly.
do: Lead the **rollout** across purchasing and run weekly sessions for colleagues.
Learn to **check** the machine's decisions and ask for a pay review.
S1.quote: Quote comparison, forecasting and supplier emails will all be software within two years.
fieldNote: Femi's mood is **calm** because his job gains from the change, but his worry is about **others**.
He expects purchasing to shrink from 25 to about 15 through natural **attrition**.

steps.text: Lead the tool rollout across the purchasing team
Run weekly training sessions for colleagues
Ask for a pay review and a lead title

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is the moment to move fast, but carefully. To friends I'd say we need shared ownership and public support, urgently, because the gains will pile up in a few companies. Online I'd say tax the gains and pay people through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's different this time. Full AGI means the machine can do my judgement too, not only my admin. My edge is I know the tools, but when the tools can do everything, that edge is thin. I'd be afraid for the whole profession and for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Day one, I'd count our money: two years of costs, and a plan. Then I'd move quickly into whatever role is left: auditing what the AI buys, or negotiating things only humans can. I'd also join a union or professional group pushing for retraining and income support, and I'd put the savings into assets that don't depend on one salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and also strangely curious. I'm building the thing that replaces me, in a way. That's a weird feeling, and I can't stop being interested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what's the first thing you'd do on day one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Camila (my partner) is a physio, so she works with her hands and has about three more years than I do. That's a real cushion for us, and I'd say it's the thing that stops me being panicked. It also makes me wonder how it feels for people whose partners work at desks too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Camila's job as a physiotherapist change your thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Day one is a spreadsheet: what we'd need to live on if my pay stopped in 18 months. Day two is a conversation with my boss at Brightwire about where the company sees my role. I'd rather ask early than find out late.

say: This is the moment to move fast but **carefully**.
We need **shared ownership** and public support, because the gains will pile up in a few firms.
think: Full AGI can do my **judgement** too, so my edge from knowing the tools is thin.
I'm building the thing that **replaces** me, and I'm still curious.
do: Count two years of **costs** and plan for pay stopping in 18 months.
Join a **union** or professional group pushing for retraining and income support.
feel: **Anxious** and strangely curious at the same time.
S2.quote: I'm building the thing that replaces me, in a way. That's a weird feeling, and I can't stop being interested.
fieldNote: Femi's **curiosity** survives even when he sees the threat, which is typical of his adaptive nature.
Camila's hands-on work gives them about **three years** more, which keeps him from panic.

steps.text: Work out what the household needs if my pay stops
Ask my boss at Brightwire where my role goes
Join a professional group pushing for retraining money
Move into auditing what the AI buys

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is enough if we get moving, so let's plan seriously. To friends I'd say put the effort into skills that stay human. Online I'd say fund retraining and make people shareholders in the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a runway. I'd probably go from buyer to someone who designs and checks the buying systems, and that could be a decent job for a few years. After that I'm not sure, and I'd be honest about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a course in AI systems or data engineering, to be a person who builds these tools, not just uses them. I'd save aggressively, maybe a third of my pay. And I'd start a small side project, maybe selling a purchasing tool to smaller distributors, to see if I can earn from what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, with a knot at the back. It's a challenge more than a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in those five years that you couldn't do in two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, I'd be scrambling. With five years, I can actually switch to a different kind of work, and Camila and I can plan the mortgage and the studies properly. It changes things from panic to project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your children anything different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids Noa and Teo to learn how to learn, and to be good with people. I'd stop pushing them to be the best at tests, because machines will beat them. I'd say to enjoy what they enjoy.

say: Five years is enough if we **get moving**, so let's plan seriously.
Make people **shareholders** in the gains and fund retraining.
think: Five years is a **runway** to go from buyer to someone who designs and checks buying systems.
After that I'm **not sure**, and I'd admit that.
do: Take a course in **data engineering** to build these tools, not only use them.
Save a **third of my pay** and start a side project selling a buying tool.
feel: Pretty **good**, with a knot at the back.
S3.quote: With five years, I can actually switch to a different kind of work
fieldNote: Femi treats five years as a **project**, not a panic, and plans a side venture.
He is honest about the **limits** of his plan after year five.

steps.text: Take a data engineering course in the evenings
Save a third of my pay each month
Start selling a buying tool to smaller distributors
Teach Noa and Teo to learn how to learn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, a decade's time, so let's do it properly. To friends I'd say get involved in the change, don't wait. Online I'd say stop arguing about whether, start planning how, and share the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not scared, and I know that could be arrogance. I'll be 53 by 2036. I have time to move into building or owning something, and my cushion is strong. It's the world around me I think about more than myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI heavily and look for the next layer: maybe running a small buying business for niche electronics, using the tools to do the work of ten. I'd invest steadily and teach what I know. I'd also write a short guide for Brightwire on how the buyers should use the tools, since sharing helps everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with a worry about fairness. A decade is a long time to get it wrong for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a decade that most people wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start my own thing while I still have a salary behind me. Most people wait until they must, which is the worst time. I've got the skills, the savings and the curiosity, so I'd rather try early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your employer to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Brightwire to say plainly what they plan, and to fund training every year, not once. I'd want staff to share in the gains, through profit shares or shares in the company. If the machine does the work, some of the pay should go to the people who trained it.

say: Stop arguing about **whether** and start planning how, and share the gains.
A decade is time to do it **properly**.
think: I'm not scared, and I know that could be **arrogance**.
It's the world around me I think about more than **myself**.
do: Start a small **niche buying business** while I still have a salary behind me.
Write a **guide** for Brightwire buyers on using the tools.
S4.quote: If the machine does the work, some of the pay should go to the people who trained it.
fieldNote: Femi's mood is **calm** because he has skills, savings and time, and he knows the risk of arrogance.
He wants **staff to share** in the gains, a clear progressive theme.

steps.text: Start a small niche buying business on the side
Invest steadily in index funds each month
Write a guide to the tools for Brightwire buyers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because even someone like me with the tools has only a thin edge when machines do all the thinking. What would help is shared ownership of the gains, paid retraining, and an income floor while people switch. I'd also want companies to stop treating their buyers as costs to be cut and start training them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm in the lucky group: young enough, skilled enough, married to someone with hands-on work. I try to remember that most people aren't.

headlineQuote: I'm in the lucky group: young enough, skilled enough, married to someone with hands-on work.
portrait: Femi is a 43-year-old lead **electronics buyer** at Brightwire Components, with a physio partner, two kids and a mortgage.
He is progressive and **adaptive**: he uses AI every day, has built his own reorder script and runs sessions for colleagues.
His mood is calm in mild worlds and **anxious** when AGI is two years away, but his curiosity never switches off.
He wants **shared ownership**, paid retraining and an income floor, and plans side ventures as a hedge.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because the edge from knowing the tools is thin once machines think.
whatWouldHelp: Shared **ownership** of the gains, paid retraining, and an income floor during switches.
